findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £1.377m underspend, but £0.956m relates to contractually committed work not yet completed.
findings.detail: Capital outturn was £2.825m against a revised budget of £4.202m. Of the £1.377m variance, £0.956m represents contractually committed expenditure awaiting completion and £0.553m is proposed carry forward. Only £0.132m represents actual overspends on demand-led schemes.
findings.matters: Shows project delivery timing constraints and procurement challenges, but the commitment is real and spending will follow. Important for understanding capital investment trajectory.
findings.figures: £1.377m total variance, £0.956m contractually committed, £0.553m carry forward, £0.132m overspends
findings.quote: Of the £1.377m variance, £0.956m relates to contractually committed expenditure and a further £0.553m is proposed for carry forward into 2026/27 to enable approved projects to be completed.

findings.headline: External audit fees increased by £105k, only partially offset by a £46.8k audit grant, signalling rising compliance costs.
findings.detail: The Strategy, Finance & Policy portfolio recorded £105k pressure on external audit fees. The council received £46.8k in audit grant funding but still faced a net pressure. This reflects rising external audit costs across the sector.
findings.matters: Rising audit fees reduce financial flexibility and are a structural cost increase with limited council control. They reflect market-wide cost inflation in audit services.
findings.figures: £105k pressure, £46.8k grant received, net pressure of approximately £58k
findings.quote: £105k pressure on external audit fees, partially offset by a £46.8k audit grant

findings.headline: Waste contract inflation of £255k, driven by green waste collection introduction and ongoing cost pressures, was offset only by profit-sharing arrangements.
findings.detail: The Rochford Norse waste contract generated a £255k overspend, attributed partly to the introduction of green waste collection service expansion. This was mitigated by £136k profit-share income from 2024/25 and favourable recycling market conditions, but these are contingent and cannot be relied upon annually.
findings.matters: Waste is the largest operational budget area (£4.4m). Structural contract inflation combined with service expansion shows cost pressure that requires ongoing mitigation through external factors (market conditions, profit-sharing).
findings.figures: £255k overspend on contract, £136k profit-share income, recycling disposal improved by £346k due to decreased cost per tonne
findings.quote: £255k overspend on Rochford Norse waste contract, partly due to the introduction of green waste collection

findings.headline: Housing Benefits payments exceeded budget by £111k, signalling demand-driven cost pressure.
findings.detail: The Communities, Wellbeing & Housing portfolio reported a negative variance on Housing Benefits Payments, with actual costs outrunning the budget expectation. This is a structural cost driver rather than an operational variance.
findings.matters: Housing Benefits are demand-led and volatile; costs rising above budget forecast indicates either higher caseloads or higher benefit levels than anticipated. This is a cost area with limited council control.
findings.figures: £111k negative variance on Housing Benefits Payments
findings.quote: £111k negative variance in relation to Housing Benefits

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 67% of approved budget, with £1.377m underspend attributed to timing delays
findings.detail: Capital expenditure of £2.825m was delivered against an approved budget of £4.202m, resulting in a net underspend of £1.377m (33% of budget). The Council attributes this to 'timing of project delivery rather than cancellation of approved schemes', with £0.956m of contractually committed expenditure and £0.553m proposed to carry forward to 2026/27. However, the variance remains substantial and warrants monitoring.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor capital delivery as a measure of execution capability and financial health, with significant variances requiring explanation and indicating potential delivery or cash flow planning challenges.
findings.figures: £2.825m outturn vs £4.202m budget; underspend of £1.377m (33% of approved programme); £0.956m committed; £0.553m carry forward
findings.quote: The Council delivered capital expenditure of £2.825m during 2025/26 against a latest approved programme of £4.202m, resulting in a net underspend of £1.377m. The variance largely reflects the timing of project delivery rather than cancellation of approved schemes.

findings.headline: Investment income significantly outperformed budget by £409k on strong cash position and high interest rates
findings.detail: The Council's £23.424m investment portfolio, held with UK local authorities, generated investment income of £1.273m compared to budgeted £864k—a 48% outperformance. This surplus was driven by favourable market rates (Bank Rate 4.50% to 3.75%) and strong cash balances, with the paper noting 'investment returns significantly above long-term averages'. The additional £409k income contributed materially to the overall revenue underspend.
findings.matters: Demonstrates strong treasury management and adequate liquidity, but sustainability is at risk as interest rates continue falling and returns normalise.
findings.figures: £1.273m investment income vs £864k budget (£409k surplus); Bank Rate 4.50% to 3.75%; total investments £23.424m
findings.quote: Investment income achieved during the year was £1.273 million compared with a budget of £864,000, generating an additional £409,000 of income for the Council and making a significant contribution to the overall revenue underspend reported for the year.

findings.headline: Procurement waiver process requirements are not consistently met—approval documentation and officer signatures missing.
findings.detail: Of three waivers reviewed, two lacked documented evidence that procurement or financial advice was sought before approval, and two were not signed by the requesting officer. This weakens the audit trail for procurement bypasses.
findings.matters: Waivers are formal exceptions to competitive procurement; missing evidence and approvals suggest inadequate oversight of this control bypass mechanism.
findings.figures: 2 of 3 waivers without advice documentation; 2 of 3 unsigned by requesting officer
findings.quote: In two cases, there was no documented evidence that procurement, legal, financial, or professional advice was sought prior to the waiver being submitted for approval.

findings.headline: Two high-value contracts (£100k Flood Risk Assessment, £216k Car Park Resurfacing) began service delivery before contracts were signed.
findings.detail: Both EPP procurements proceeded to service provision without signed contracts in place at the time of audit testing. One also had no documented due diligence on the supplier (the £216k car park project).
findings.matters: Operating without signed contracts exposes the council to disputes over scope, payment terms, and liabilities, and signals weak contract execution discipline.
findings.figures: £100,000 (Flood Risk Assessment); £216,000 (Car Park Resurfacing)
findings.quote: For both cases, the contract was not signed at the time of testing , yet the service provision has started.

findings.headline: A £415k contract (Acclaim Contracts Ltd, Clements Hall) was awarded without documented due diligence and without evidence spend was in approved budget.
findings.detail: Testing of procurements found no evidence that due diligence checks were completed on the supplier before award, and no evidence that the £415,357.56 spend was within the approved budget. This represents a significant control gap on a material contract.
findings.matters: Supplier financial standing and governance risks are not assessed before award, and budget approvals are not evidenced—both are core financial controls.
findings.quote: there was no evidence that due diligence was completed on the supplier and documented. In addition, there is no evidence that the spend is within the approved budget.

findings.headline: The contract register is incomplete, missing critical data on 73% of contracts tested.
findings.detail: Only 27% of 85 contracts have awarded value documented, 31% have start/end dates, 8% have a contract number, and 11% have route to market noted. The register is still being developed, with ongoing work to reconcile against expenditure data and service areas.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess the council's contractual exposure or liabilities if the contract register does not show what contracts exist, their values, or terms.
findings.figures: 23 of 85 contracts (27%) have contract value; 26 of 85 (31%) have dates; 7 of 85 (8%) have contract number; 9 of 85 (11%) have route to market
findings.quote: Awarded contract value is documented for 23 contracts (27%) while annual spend is recorded for 84 (99%).

findings.headline: Control effectiveness is Limited, with testing unable to verify compliance across multiple procurements due to unavailable evidence.
findings.detail: The audit assessed control design as Moderate but operational effectiveness as Limited. Significant gaps were found in policy compliance, record retention, and structured reporting. The council is operating during transition to new partnership procurement rules, creating additional compliance risk.
findings.matters: Limited operational control over procurement suggests financial governance weaknesses that would concern lenders reviewing council robustness.
findings.figures: Design Opinion: Moderate; Effectiveness Opinion: Limited
findings.quote: The control effectiveness is assessed as Limited because , we were unable to complete testing for some sampled procurements /contracts due to unavailable evidence.

findings.headline: Counter-fraud capacity is limited and reliant on support arrangements, creating potential resilience risk.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges having limited dedicated internal counter-fraud capacity and relies on external support arrangements. The statement flags this as creating a potential resilience issue, and commits to review whether counter-fraud arrangements remain proportionate and ensure fraud risk is considered through internal audit, risk management and service controls.
findings.matters: A council with limited counter-fraud capacity may not detect financial irregularities; this increases fraud and loss risk, which affects the council's financial position and a lender's security.
findings.figures: Limited dedicated internal counter-fraud capacity
findings.quote: Fraud remains a significant public sector risk. Rochford has limited dedicated internal counter-fraud capacity and relies on support arrangements. This creates a potential resilience issue.

findings.headline: Officer capacity and retention pressures are heightened by Local Government Reorganisation and recruitment challenges.
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that governance framework resilience depends on having sufficient officer capacity, capability and resilience across key areas including finance, procurement, risk management, health and safety and ICT. These capacity risks are heightened by Local Government Reorganisation, recruitment and retention pressures alongside the need to deliver business-as-usual transformation activity.
findings.matters: A council with recruitment and retention problems during a reorganisation period has reduced capacity to manage financial controls, audit readiness, and risk; this affects the council's ability to maintain governance standards.
findings.figures: Heightened by Local Government Reorganisation, recruitment and retention pressures
findings.quote: The Council's governance framework depends on having sufficient officer capacity, capability and resilience. This includes corporate governance, finance, procurement, risk management, health and safety, ICT, information governance and democratic support. Capacity risks are heightened by Local Government Reorganisation, recruitment and retention pressures and the need to deliver business-as-usual alongside transformation activity.

findings.headline: Health and Safety governance received Limited assurance on both design and effectiveness, identified as the council's most significant governance issue.
findings.detail: Internal audit found Limited assurance for health and safety control framework, indicating weaknesses in design and operation including responsibilities, processes, monitoring and assurance. The council treats this as a significant governance priority for 2026/27 given the statutory nature of health and safety responsibilities, and commits to implement management actions to clarify ownership, update controls and strengthen reporting.
findings.matters: Weak health and safety governance creates liability exposure for the council and indicates broader control framework weaknesses; a lender needs assurance that the council can manage statutory obligations and operational risks.
findings.figures: Limited assurance over both design and effectiveness
findings.quote: Health and safety is the most significant Rochford-specific governance issue identified through the evidence reviewed. The Limited assurance opinion over both design and effectiveness means that the Council needs to strengthen the framework and its operation.

findings.headline: Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a challenging financial environment with multiple medium-term sustainability risks.
findings.detail: The council's MTFS faces significant headwinds from funding reform, business rates reset, collection fund volatility, inflationary pressures, demand pressures and Local Government Reorganisation. The council acknowledges the need to continue ensuring budget setting is supported by robust estimates, adequate reserves, transparent assumptions and clear Section 151 Officer assurance.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's forward funding environment; multiple concurrent pressures on income (rates reset, funding reform, collection volatility) create uncertainty about financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Funding reform, business rates reset, collection fund volatility, inflationary pressures, demand pressures and Local Government Reorganisation
findings.quote: The Council's Medium-Term Financial Strategy identifies a challenging financial environment. Funding reform, business rates reset, collection fund volatility, inflationary pressures, demand pressures and Local Government Reorganisation all create risks to medium-term financial sustainability.

findings.headline: 2024/25 audit of accounts was disclaimed, requiring sustained improvement in financial reporting and audit readiness.
findings.detail: The council's external audit for 2024/25 was disclaimed in the context of national audit reset arrangements. The council acknowledges this means it must continue to rebuild audit assurance through improved financial reporting, evidence, reconciliations, working papers and audit readiness over future cycles. The statement identifies specific areas requiring improvement including timely production of draft accounts, complete audit working papers, clear audit trails, and robust reconciliations.
findings.matters: A lender cannot rely on assured financial statements if the audit is disclaimed; this undermines the council's financial credibility and increases the risk of undetected issues in the accounts.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit disclaimed
findings.quote: The audit report for Rochford's 2024/25 accounts was disclaimed. A disclaimed audit opinion does not, by itself, mean that the Council has no governance framework. However, it is a significant part of the financial governance environment and must be treated transparently within the AGS.

findings.headline: Cyber Security in the Supply Chain audit identified immature supplier risk management
findings.detail: Cyber Security in the Supply Chain received Limited assurance with 2 high significance findings: inconsistent assessment of supplier cyber risks and an immature approach to supplier risk management overall.
findings.matters: Weak supplier cyber risk assessment could expose the council to operational disruption or data breach via third parties, affecting service continuity and reputation.
findings.figures: 2 high significance findings; Limited assurance opinion
findings.quote: Cyber Security in the Supply Chain (2) – Inconsistent assessment of supplier cyber security risks and an immature approach to supplier risk management

findings.headline: Health and Safety audit received Limited assurance due to out of date policies and incomplete site register
findings.detail: Health and Safety received Limited assurance on both design and effectiveness with 2 high significance findings: out of date policies and procedures, and an incomplete operational site register.
findings.matters: Outdated H&S policies and incomplete asset registers create regulatory compliance risk and potential liability exposure for the council.
findings.figures: 2 high significance findings; Limited assurance opinion
findings.quote: Health and Safety (2) – out of date policies/procedures and incomplete operational site register.

findings.headline: Procurement and Contract Management received Limited assurance with an incomplete contracts register
findings.detail: This area received only Limited assurance on both control design and operational effectiveness, with an incomplete contracts register cited as a high significance finding. Limited assurance means significant gaps exist in procedures and controls.
findings.matters: An incomplete contracts register is a material internal control weakness in a financially significant area; it prevents management and auditors from knowing what commitments the council has entered into.
findings.figures: 1 high significance finding; Limited assurance opinion
findings.quote: Procurement and Contract Management (1) – Incomplete contracts register.

findings.headline: Four audit recommendations remain overdue, blamed on competing work priorities
findings.detail: Of 39 recommendations followed up during the year, 35 were fully implemented but 4 were not implemented and now classed as overdue. BDO identifies 'competing work priorities' as the common reason actions were not completed on time. This suggests either resource constraints or management bandwidth issues.
findings.matters: Inability or unwillingness to close audit findings on time indicates management capacity concerns or competing pressures that could affect the council's ability to execute other commitments.
findings.figures: 35 of 39 recommendations fully implemented; 4 now overdue
findings.quote: A common theme for why actions were not completed on time was due to competing work priorities.

findings.headline: Audit opinion is Moderate, not Substantial, for both design and effectiveness
findings.detail: The audit concluded that while the Council has a generally sound governance framework and budget setting guidance, gaps exist in formal documentation of the end-to-end MTFS methodology. Control effectiveness is assessed as moderate because while controls largely operate as intended, regular detailed self-assessment against CIPFA guidance has not been embedded.
findings.matters: A lender would expect Substantial assurance on financial planning controls, not Moderate. The gap suggests the Council's financial planning framework, while functional, has structural resilience risks.
findings.figures: Design Opinion: Moderate. Effectiveness Opinion: Moderate.
findings.quote: Overall, we have provided the Council with moderate assurance over both the design and operational effectiveness of the controls in place to support the development, monitoring and approval of the MTFS.

findings.headline: CIPFA guidance compliance assessment not embedded as regular process
findings.detail: The Council completed a one-off self-assessment against CIPFA Financial Management Code in January 2026, but this is not yet embedded within the annual budget setting process. The assessment was presented only as a high-level summary rather than detailed evidence of compliance, creating risk that weaknesses in financial management could go unidentified.
findings.matters: Regular detailed self-assessment against best practice standards helps identify emerging financial management weaknesses before they cause problems; one-off high-level reviews provide insufficient assurance.
findings.figures: Self-assessment completed January 2026, presented February 2026; no regular cycle established.
findings.quote: the results were presented only as a high level summary and the exercise is not yet embedded within the annual budget setting and MTFS process

findings.headline: MTFS development process lacks formal documented methodology
findings.detail: The Council has budget setting guidance and established governance forums, but no single formally documented end-to-end methodology for developing the MTFS. The process relies on organizational knowledge held by officers rather than standardized documented procedures, and lacks documented evidence of source documents, key personnel meetings, information inputs, and independent management review.
findings.matters: Without formal documentation, MTFS processes may be applied inconsistently if key staff leave, reducing transparency and reliability of financial projections that a lender depends on.
findings.figures: No specific financial impact quantified, but recommendation due by December 2026.
findings.quote: there is no single formally documented methodology setting out the end to end process for its development and review. Hence, the MTFS process is reliant on organisational and officer retained knowledge

findings.headline: No corporate aggregation or monitoring of risk assessments, inspection outcomes and remedial actions—council cannot demonstrate compliance
findings.detail: The council lacks a comprehensive corporate process for aggregating, monitoring, reviewing and reporting risk assessments, inspection outcomes and remedial actions. As a result, risk assessments and inspection outcomes cannot be readily provided for multiple council-managed sites. The audit notes that this deficiency 'undermines effective oversight by the Health, Safety and Wellbeing Committee and the CLT' and means 'the Council risks failing to address known hazards completing necessary remedial works, increasing the likelihood of accidents or incidents that could harm employees or the public.' This also poses potential legal and regulatory consequences, including fines and penalties.
findings.matters: Without corporate tracking and reporting of H&S compliance, the council cannot demonstrate it meets statutory obligations. This is regulatory and financial risk.
findings.figures: Multiple sites where current risk assessments and inspections could not be readily provided, including: Windmill (Grade II listed building), Freight House (event space), Hall Road Cemetery, Hullbridge Senior Citizens day centre, Castle Hall, Rochford Park, Rawreth recreation ground.
findings.quote: Risk assessments, inspection outcomes and remedial works completed are not routinely aggregated or monitored corporately by the Health and Safety service. There is no process to aggregate or monitor the outstanding remedial works

findings.headline: Council lacks a comprehensive site register and cannot identify all premises where it has statutory H&S duties
findings.detail: The audit identified that the council has no complete operational site register of all premises, sites and spaces (including leased properties) for which it holds statutory H&S duties. The auditors found only 7 sites initially listed, then identified others including Cherry Orchard Country Park, cemeteries, and waste/recycling operations. The Asset Management Team only provided a full asset list late during the audit. This gap means the council struggles to demonstrate documentary evidence of statutory compliance across all locations.
findings.matters: A council that cannot identify all the premises it is legally responsible for faces unquantified legal and financial exposure. This is a fundamental control failure.
findings.figures: Initial list: 7 sites. Additional sites identified: Cherry Orchard Jubilee Country Park, Hall Road Cemetery, Great Wakering waste and recycling, and others.
findings.quote: The absence of a clear, comprehensive operational site register detailing all premises, sites, and spaces, including leased properties and the service areas, for which the Council holds a statutory duty for Health and Safety meant our review was unable to select a sample of them in accordance with BDO methodology.

findings.headline: Auditors gave Limited assurance on both H&S control design and effectiveness, meaning objectives are at risk
findings.detail: The independent auditors (BDO) assessed both the design of controls and their operational effectiveness as Limited. This is a significant governance finding: the council's system of internal controls for Health and Safety is weakened, with key objectives at risk of not being achieved. Non-compliance with key procedures and controls places the system objectives at risk.
findings.matters: Limited audit opinion indicates material control gaps in a safety-critical area; lenders assess governance and compliance risk, and this directly flags both.
findings.figures: Design Opinion: Limited. Effectiveness Opinion: Limited.
findings.quote: We have provided Limited Assurance over both the design and effectiveness of the controls in place to manage Health and Safety.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Rochford District Council Provisional audit planning report Year ending 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Documentation and timeliness of audit evidence provision remains below required standard
findings.detail: The 2024/25 assessment identified that improvements are required in 'The timely provision of working papers and audit evidence in line with the agreed Client Assistance Schedule and timetable.' This suggests the council is not delivering audit evidence on schedule, delaying the audit process.
findings.matters: Late delivery of evidence delays audit completion, increases audit costs, and suggests weak financial management discipline and capacity. For lenders, it indicates the finance team may lack capacity or capability to handle complex accounting matters.
findings.figures: Working papers and evidence delivery marked as 'Requires improvements' in 2024/25 audit assessment
findings.quote: The timely provision of working papers and audit evidence in line with the agreed Client Assistance Schedule and timetable... Requires improvements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Rochford District Council Provisional audit planning report Year ending 31 March 2026
findings.headline: New CIPFA Bulletin 22 valuation requirements add complexity during period of demonstrated valuation weakness
findings.detail: For 2025/26, the council is required to implement CIPFA Bulletin 22, which mandates a quinquennial revaluation or five-year rolling programme for formal valuations, supported by annual indexation. The auditor has specifically flagged this as a risk, noting: 'Successful implementation will depend on the Council ensuring that their existing valuation programme is adapted in line with the guidance and that appropriate indices are selected to be applied in intervening years.'
findings.matters: The council has just demonstrated it cannot manage the current valuation regime. Introducing new, more complex requirements during a period of proved weakness creates material risk of further errors and continued audit failures.
findings.figures: CIPFA Bulletin 22 requires quinquennial revaluation or five-year rolling programme; applies to PPE of £50m
findings.quote: In the 2025/26 Financial Statements the Council will be required to apply CIPFA Bulletin 22 which reassesses the current regime of valuation for non-investment assets across the public sector. The guidance mandates a quinquennial revaluation or a five-year rolling programme for formal valuations, supported by annual indexation in the intervening years. Successful implementation will depend on the Council ensuring that their existing valuation programme is adapted in line with the guidance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Rochford District Council Provisional audit planning report Year ending 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Opening reserves balances for 2025/26 will have only limited assurance due to unresolved prior-year gaps
findings.detail: The auditor expects to have only limited assurance over opening balances for 2025/26 and limited assurance over closing reserves balances due to uncertainty over the opening amount. The council's usable and unusable reserves remain dependent on completing a work programme to rebuild assurance, which will not be completed in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Uncertainty over opening and closing reserves means the council cannot reliably demonstrate how much cash and resources it actually has available. This is critical for understanding whether the council can fund services and meet obligations.
findings.figures: Limited assurance only over opening and closing reserve balances; no historic rebuild work scheduled for 2025/26
findings.quote: We will have limited assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26; and Limited assurance over the closing reserves balance, due to uncertainty over the opening amount. It is therefore critical that Management ensure they can provide high quality working papers, robust audit evidence, and resolve the underlying issues identified in prior years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Rochford District Council Provisional audit planning report Year ending 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Property, Plant & Equipment (PPE) of £50m remains unaudited due to valuation evidence failures
findings.detail: The auditor was unable to obtain sufficient and appropriate evidence to support PPE asset values and could not corroborate key assumptions applied by the valuer. This is the reason for the disclaimer opinions. The council's 2024/25 audit resulted in no assurance over the PPE balance. The 2024/25 assessment flagged this as an area 'Requiring improvements' with the specific note that 'We could not corroborate the assumptions and inputs for the valuation methodology of the Council's assets we selected for testing.'
findings.matters: PPE at £50m represents the largest asset on the balance sheet. Inability to verify valuations creates fundamental uncertainty about asset quality, potential impairments, and the council's net asset position.
findings.figures: Property, plant and equipment: £50 million; relating to land and buildings, including council dwellings: £40.4 million; Additions totalled: £3.1 million
findings.quote: In respect of the valuation of Property, Plant and Equipment, we were unable to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence to support the asset values. As a result, we were unable to corroborate the key assumptions applied by the valuer.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Rochford District Council Provisional audit planning report Year ending 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Council has received disclaimer opinions for two consecutive years and audit evidence gaps remain unresolved
findings.detail: Rochford received disclaimer opinions in 2023/24 and 2024/25, meaning auditors could not form any opinion on the Financial Statements. The council's progress in rebuilding assurance is described as falling 'behind the expected timescales' in NAO guidance. The auditor has decided not to commence rebuilding assurance over pre-2023/24 balances during 2025/26.
findings.matters: Disclaimer opinions mean the accounts cannot be relied upon and indicate fundamental control or evidence problems. For lenders, this signals material uncertainty about the true financial position and governance capability.
findings.figures: Disclaimer opinions issued in 2023/24 and 2024/25; no rebuilding of historic assurance planned for 2025/26
findings.quote: In the audit reports for the years ended 31 March 2024 and 31 March 2025, a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the application of the backstop. In our view, the Council's progress falls behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Capital and Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Finance lease liabilities of £2.775m will be serviced over 21 years, representing a fixed long-term obligation on the council's balance sheet
findings.detail: The council has lease liabilities of £2.775m at 31 March 2025 arising from IFRS 16 implementation. These will be written down on an annuity basis over 21 years. While the underlying cash flows were being paid before IFRS 16, these liabilities now occupy the council's debt capacity.
findings.matters: Lease liabilities represent fixed obligations that constrain the council's financial flexibility and must be considered as part of overall debt limits and affordability.
findings.figures: £2.775m lease liability at 31 March 2025; 21-year repayment period
findings.quote: The outstanding lease liability on the IFRS 16 basis was £2.775 million at 31 March 2025. This will be reduced on an annuity basis for the next 21 years until it reaches zero.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Capital and Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council estimates each £1m borrowed will create approximately £62k annual revenue charge, meaning planned £4.4m internal borrowing will cost £272k per annum
findings.detail: The strategy includes a forward-looking calculation of revenue implications: borrowing £1m at current rates with 50-year MRP straight-line creates ~£62k annual revenue cost. The planned £4.4m internal borrowing for 2026/27 will therefore create an ongoing revenue commitment of approximately £272k per annum.
findings.matters: As the council shifts to funding capital from borrowing rather than cash, the resulting revenue charges (interest and MRP) will constrain services and reduce budget flexibility in future years.
findings.figures: £62k per £1m borrowed per annum at current rates over 50 years
findings.quote: each £1 million borrowed would result in a charge to revenue per annum of approximately £62k at current interest rates and assuming straight line MRP over 50 years

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Capital and Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Largest capital project, Clements Hall investment of £3.48m, sits alongside material capital programme delivery risks rated as Amber
findings.detail: The capital programme includes Clements Hall (£3.48m), Mill Hall (£1.696m), and Rayleigh Leisure Centre (£920k). The risk register identifies capital programme delivery risks (cost increases, delays, overspends) as a key concern, with initial risk score of 20 (Red), revised to 15 (Amber) after mitigation.
findings.matters: Large individual projects create execution risk. Overruns on these schemes could consume additional budget, defer other services, or require additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Clements Hall investment £3.48m; Mill Hall £1.696m; Rayleigh Leisure Centre £920k
findings.quote: Increased costs resulting in greater demand on budgets than anticipated, delivery but at a lower standard than planned meaning service outcomes might be compromised

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Capital and Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Capital programme depends on £650k in capital receipts that may not be realised, with projects deferred or cancelled if receipts fall short
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme of £10.2m is financed from capital receipts (£650k), grants (£670k), revenue contributions (£4.45m) and internal borrowing (£4.4m). The strategy explicitly states capital receipts are assumed realisable but may not be, in which case projects will either be delayed, cancelled, or funded by additional borrowing.
findings.matters: A material portion of planned capital delivery depends on asset sales that are uncertain. Failure to realise receipts will either defer council priorities or force additional borrowing, worsening the council's debt position.
findings.figures: Capital receipts £650k (2026/27); capital receipts £1,366k (2025/26)
findings.quote: The capital receipts are assumed to be realisable at this stage. Should this not be the case then projects will either be funded by borrowing, delayed until capital receipts become available or cancelled.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Capital and Investment Strategy 2026/27
findings.headline: Council's cash reserves will become insufficient for capital spending at current rates, forcing future external borrowing
findings.detail: The liability benchmark shows the council using internal borrowing of £4.846m in 2026/27 and declining thereafter, but the strategy explicitly warns that if capital investment continues at current levels without replenishment of cash resources, external borrowing will be required. The council has no external debt currently but is forecast to deplete reserves significantly.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt trajectory and when it will be forced to take on external borrowing. This signals a constraint on financial flexibility and growing reliance on debt markets.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £4.846m (2026/27); capital programme £10.2m (2026/27) vs £4.1m (2025/26)
findings.quote: should capital investment continue at current rates and continue to be funded entirely from cash resources unless those resources are replenished the council will have to consider external borrowing to finance capital expenditure in the future

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme delivered £1.377m underspend, but £0.956m relates to contractually committed work not yet completed.
news_drafts.lead: Shows project delivery timing constraints and procurement challenges, but the commitment is real and spending will follow. Important for understanding capital investment trajectory.

news_drafts.headline: External audit fees increased by £105k, only partially offset by a £46.8k audit grant, signalling rising compliance costs.
news_drafts.lead: Rising audit fees reduce financial flexibility and are a structural cost increase with limited council control. They reflect market-wide cost inflation in audit services.

news_drafts.headline: Waste contract inflation of £255k, driven by green waste collection introduction and ongoing cost pressures, was offset only by profit-sharing arrangements.
news_drafts.lead: Waste is the largest operational budget area (£4.4m). Structural contract inflation combined with service expansion shows cost pressure that requires ongoing mitigation through external factors (market conditions, profit-sharing).
